bib.title: BLEU: a Method for Automatic Evaluation of Machine Translation
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 40th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), Philadelphia, pp. 311-318

question: Can a quick, cheap, language-independent automatic metric based on n-gram overlap with reference translations rank machine translation systems the way human judges do?
hypothesis: The closer a machine translation is to professional human reference translations, the better it is, so a numerical closeness metric averaged over a corpus should correlate highly with human judgment.
contributions: BLEU: geometric mean of clipped (modified) n-gram precisions times a corpus-level brevity penalty
Evidence that BLEU ranks 5 systems (3 MT, 2 human) in the same order as monolingual and bilingual human judges (r=0.99, 0.96)

method.summary: Defines BLEU as the geometric mean of modified n-gram precisions (n up to 4, uniform weights) times an exponential brevity penalty computed over the whole corpus. Scores 3 commercial MT systems and 2 human translators on a 500-sentence Chinese-English news set against 2 references, tests differences with paired t-tests on 20 blocks, and regresses mean human ratings on BLEU.
method.task: automatic evaluation of machine translation (Chinese to English)

datasets.name: Chinese-English news test corpus
datasets.size: about 500 sentences (40 general news stories); 4 reference translations per sentence available
datasets.split: 20 blocks of 25 sentences for variance; Fig 1 used 127 source sentences with 4 references

datasets.name: Human judgment subset
datasets.size: 250 source-translation pairs (5 translations of a random subset of the 500 sentences)
datasets.source: 10 monolingual native English judges, 10 bilingual native Chinese judges, none professional translators

models.name: H1, H2
models.architecture: human translators: H1 lacks native proficiency in both Chinese and English; H2 is a native English speaker

inference.samples: one output per system per sentence; 20 blocks of 25 sentences used for variance

parameters.brevity penalty: BP = 1 if c > r, else exp(1 - r/c); r = sum of best-match (closest) reference lengths per candidate sentence, c = total candidate length

metrics.name: BLEU
metrics.definition: BP * exp(sum_{n=1..N} w_n log p_n), p_n = corpus-level clipped n-gram precision

metrics.name: Human rating
metrics.definition: each translation rated 1 (very bad) to 5 (very good); monolingual judges rate readability and fluency only

metrics.name: Pearson-style correlation coefficient of linear regression of human score on BLEU

baselines: arithmetic mean instead of geometric mean (reported slightly weaker)
eval.protocol: Paired t-test between adjacent systems on 20 blocks of 25 sentences; paired t-tests (95% CI) on per-judge rating differences between adjacent systems; single-reference simulation picks one of 4 references at random per story.

limits: Sentence-level scores often differ from human judgment; BLEU only claimed valid averaged over a test corpus (footnote 4).

Validated on 5 systems (3 MT, 2 human) of one language pair (Chinese-English) and one 500-sentence set; correlations rest on n=5 points. A cited companion study covers Arabic, Chinese, French, Spanish.
Score depends on number of references, so scores with different reference counts are not comparable.
Geometric mean is harsh if any modified precision is zero; authors assume this is rare for corpora of reasonable size and N<=4.
No recall term; no handling of synonyms or concepts. Only case folding as normalisation, tokenisation not specified.
Judges were non-professionals; the bilingual group could not separate H1 from H2. Authors state summarization and other NLG 'could' be adapted, untested.
